paper_title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. Ablations provide evidence consistent with contributions from learned GUI/code coordination, scalable verifiable supervision, and action step balanced optimization, while demonstrating cross-platform transfer on WindowsAgentArena. Our project homepage is at https://os-copilot.github.io/OS-Helix/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The rapid progress of vision-language models (VLMs) (Team, 2026; Wang et al., 2025b; Team et al., 2026a; Anthropic, 2025; Zeng et al., 2026; OpenAI, 2025; Bai et al., 2026; Zou et al., 2026) has accelerated the development of computer-using agents (CUAs), which aim to execute open-ended tasks in human-facing digital environments. Most existing CUAs formulate digital automation as graphical interaction, where agents perceive screenshots, reason over interface states, and act through mouse and keyboard operations. However, GUI-centric CUAs (Liu et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2024; Feizi et al., 2026) still face practical bottlenecks in realistic desktop workflows. Visual grounding can fail on small or ambiguous interface elements, and fine-grained interaction can make structured state manipulation cumbersome even with batched actions. comFigure 1: Overview of GUI-only, codeonly, and hybrid computer use. 1 plementary interface is programmatic control, through which command-line and code agents can inspect files, access system state, and execute compound operations directly through the shell (Yang et al., 2026e; 2024; Wang et al., 2025c). Yet code execution alone cannot fully address the long tail of desktop task scenarios that depends on visual layout, application-specific UI state, or software behavior exposed only through the interface. As illustrated in Figure 1, these complementary strengths motivate single agent that coordinates GUI and code, where GUI provides general visual access to arbitrary applications while code provides efficient and precise manipulation of programmatic state. Despite this complementarity, building native hybrid GUI/code CUA remains an open problem. Simply attaching code tool to GUI model does not teach it when or why to use either modality. In our preliminary experiments, as shown in Table 14, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) achieves over 34% success on OSWorld-Verified (Xie et al., 2025) with GUI actions alone, but falls to roughly 32% when code execution is naively exposed. Prompt-level composition can therefore disrupt an existing GUI policy rather than create coordinated behavior, making it essential to internalize hybrid coordination capabilities into the model through training on high-quality hybrid data. Several existing approaches have explored hybrid execution paradigms that combine GUI interaction with code-like actions. Framework-centric systems (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a) rely on external harnesses to coordinate GUI, code, memory, and recovery; tool-call-based approaches (Jia et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Shi et al., 2026) expose programmatic operations through predefined application-specific interfaces; and model-fusion approaches (Wang et al., 2025a; Qin et al., 2025) combine complementary capabilities through predefined designs. Although these systems expand the scope of hybrid computer use, they leave open how single policy can learn the routing between the GUI and code actions through hybrid training. To address these challenges, we present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained computer-using agent that unifies GUI interaction and code execution within single policy. On the infrastructure side, we introduce applicationartifact composition, which combines versioned applications with authentic artifacts to instantiate diverse and reproducible desktop states. An Exploration Agent proposes instructions grounded in these states through brief exploration of the initialized environment, while an independent Evaluator Agent constructs task-specific, primarily rule-based evaluators. Together, this pipeline supports scalable synthesis, filtering, and collection of high-quality GUI/code trajectories for model training, thereby providing the data foundation necessary to internalize hybrid coordination capabilities into the model. On the training side, we first use filtered hybrid trajectories to internalize basic action semantics and modality routing, and then optimize the policy through online RL in executable desktop environments. In early RL experiments, we observe steady increase in the proportion of code actions accompanied by degradation in performance. We attribute this to the token-count asymmetry between short GUI actions and substantially longer code actions, which causes the optimization signal to be dominated by code steps. To address this, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which constructs the sample-level importance ratio over action steps rather than raw assistant-token counts, enabling more balanced optimization of the two modalities. These training components directly answer the open question of how single policy can natively learn to coordinate GUI and code actions through hybrid training, yielding an agent that performs strongly and reliably across diverse desktop tasks. In summary, our contributions are: 1) We formulate native GUI/code hybrid computer use as an end-to-end policy-learning problem and show through controlled experiments that merely exposing GUI policy to code execution fails to yield reliable routing, motivating the need to internalize coordination through hybrid training. 2) We introduce applicationartifact composition and decoupled instruction/evaluator synthesis pipeline to construct diverse, reproducible, executable desktop states and generate high-quality hybrid data for internalizing GUI and code execution capabilities. 3) We propose Step-balanced GSPO for the agentic RL stage of native hybrid policy training, which prevents long code actions from dominating optimization, and enables single policy to learn GUI and code coordination. 4) We will release the OS-Helix model family and research artifacts, including the desktop datasynthesis and RL environments, task and trajectory collection pipelines, approximately 9K generated 2 instructions, 83K unfiltered SFT samples, and about 31K successful filtered SFT samples in the unified GUI/code action space.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Hybrid GUI/Code Computer-Using Agents. Traditional GUI-native agents learn screenshot-toaction policies over visual interface states (Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d), whereas command-line and coding agents operate over files, shells, and programmatic state (Anthropic, 2025; OpenClaw, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; 2024). Their complementary strengths motivate hybrid computer use. Framework-centric systems (GonzalezPumariega et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2026a) coordinate GUI, code, memory, and recovery through external harnesses, often using strong proprietary models. Their performance is coupled to costly inference and hand-engineered orchestration, making the models own hybrid coordination difficult to isolate. Tool-call-based approaches (Jia et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025b; Shi et al., 2026) expose programmatic operations through predefined, application-specific interfaces, limiting coverage and transfer to available integrations and tool schemas. Some approaches integrate GUI, code, and other capabilities through model fusion (Wang et al., 2025a; Qin et al., 2025), relying on predefined fusion rather than coordination learned within single policy. Qwen-UI-Agent (Zhou et al., 2026a) also explores training with mixed GUI and code-like action capabilities, demonstrating the practical potential of native hybrid agents. However, existing studies describe data construction, executable environments, supervision, and training configurations at different levels of granularity, making controlled reproduction and comparison of learned coordination mechanisms difficult. Our work complements by studying executable applicationartifact state construction, decoupled instructionevaluator synthesis, and more stable optimization for training single GUI/code policy. Environment Scaling and Task Synthesis for Computer-Using Agents. Realistic long-horizon tasks and interactive environments are essential for training CUAs, yet manual task design and trajectory annotation are expensive and difficult to scale. This makes automated acquisition of highquality instructions and demonstrations central problem. One line of work crawls web tutorials and documentation and decomposes them into executable task instructions (Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a). Another line starts from the target environment itself and infers tasks from what the agent can observe or manipulate: Explorer (Pahuja et al., 2025) extracts and refines task intents from web entry pages, while OS-Genesis (Sun et al., 2025), GUI-ReWalk (Lin et al., 2025), TreeCUA (Jiang et al., 2026), and AUTO PLAY (Ramrakhya et al., 2026) synthesize tasks through exploratory interaction with the environment. These methods primarily scale task and trajectory synthesis, but they do not substantially scale the underlying interactive worlds, which constrains the diversity of behaviors learned by the agent. Unlike more constrained interaction domains such as web and mobile (Cao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Wu et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026), PC environments, such as Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, provide natural substrate for scalable CUA training through system-level code execution, mature application ecosystems, persistent file systems, and package managers, enabling verifiable tasks grounded in concrete system state (Sun et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026). Recent work has begun to use virtual machines to expand desktop environments and synthesize tasks (Wang et al., 2026a; Lv et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026), exploring different parts of desktop-state construction and task generation. Table 6 summarizes the reported coverage of existing task-synthesis pipelines. Existing efforts differ in the extent to which they scale applications, authentic artifacts, executable initial states, and verifiable terminal conditions. Our pipeline integrates applicationartifact composition, reproducible desktop-state construction, and environment-grounded instruction and evaluator synthesis into unified framework for scalable, verifiable desktop-task generation. Training Paradigms for Computer-Using Agents. CUA training has broadly evolved from imitation-style supervised fine-tuning toward reinforcement learning in interactive environments. SFT-based systems learn action formats, visual grounding, and task execution from human demonstrations, synthetic trajectories, web tutorials, or teacher-model rollouts (Cheng et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Sun et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). Between SFT and online interaction, offline preference-optimization methods such as DPO (Gao et al., 2026) and offline GRPO (Yang et al., 2026c) improve policies from static preference data, but remain limited by the coverage of collected trajectories and cannot directly optimize recovery under environment feedback. Online RL methods for CUAs are further split into grounding RL and agentic 3 Figure 2: Overview of the OS-Helix pipeline. Stage 1 constructs executable desktop environments by composing applications and artifacts. Stage 2 explores each environment to synthesize instructions and evaluators, yielding verifiable tasks. Stage 3 uses teacher-generated GUI/code trajectories for SFT cold start. Stage 4 performs online agentic RL in live sandboxes. RL. Grounding RL optimizes low-level GUI localization or action selection with specialized visual rewards (Lu et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026b; Tang et al., 2026a; Feizi et al., 2026). Agentic RL instead optimizes complete trajectories in executable environments with rule-based or verifiable rewards. Recent CUA work has begun to tailor the optimization algorithm to this setting: ComputerRL (Lai et al., 2026) introduces Entropulse, which alternates online RL with SFT to mitigate entropy collapse; CUA-Gym (Wang et al., 2026a) trains CUA checkpoints with GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025); and ScaleCUA (Lv et al., 2026) adopts GRPO-style RL (Shao et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026) together with frontier sampling and visual-context segmentation. EvoCUA-1.5 (Huang et al., 2026) proposes Step-Level Policy Optimization for decomposed multi-turn samples. Nevertheless, how to systematically train single policy to route between native GUI and code actions while maintaining stable optimization across heterogeneous action granularities remains underexplored. Our work addresses this setting through hybrid SFT and online agentic RL with Step-balanced GSPO, mitigating optimization imbalance and enabling more effective native coordination.

sections.content: 3.1 OVERVIEW An overview of the OS-Helix pipeline is shown in Figure 2. OS-Helix is built around simple premise: real computer-using agent should treat GUI interaction and code execution as two complementary ways of changing the same digital state. Rather than attaching shell tool to GUI model at inference time, we construct unified pipeline in which environments, instructions, trajectories, and reinforcement signals are all designed for hybrid GUI/code execution. Here, AGUI denotes GUI actions such as clicking and typing; Ameta denotes episode-level metaactions such as task termination; actions in Acode execute either Python or Bash directly in the operating system. Each code action runs in fresh process. Its stdout and stderr are appended to the current-turn context as tool response for subsequent decision-making.

sections.title: 3.2 DATA INFRASTRUCTURE
sections.content: The scale of computer-using agent training is ultimately bounded by the diversity of executable states from which meaningful tasks can arise. This is particularly important on desktops, where workflows are shaped jointly by applications, user artifacts, and persistent local state. We view authentic artifacts as natural axis for expanding this state space, with artifact types and file formats providing direct link to the applications that can operate on them. Based on this principle, we construct diverse executable desktop environments and synthesize grounded, verifiable tasks from the resulting states.

sections.title: 3.2.1 APPLICATION–ARTIFACT COMPOSITION FOR DESKTOP ENVIRONMENTS
sections.content: Real-world desktop workflows are commonly grounded in existing artifacts that are read, edited, or transformed through applications. Thus, we factor scalable desktop-environment construction into two reusable components: applications with fixed versions, launch procedures, and diverse initialization configurations, and artifacts carrying authentic content and persistent state. Their compatibilityaware composition produces executable desktop states from which realistic tasks can arise. To instantiate such states at scale, we organize artifacts and applications into an applicationartifact compatibility graph, whose edges are determined by the artifact types and file formats that applications can consume. The underlying application configuration records these supported input types, together with the version, launch commands, and initialization settings required for reproducible execution. For example, .pptx artifact can be connected to LibreOffice Impress and WPS Presentation directly, whose application configurations specify how each application is launched with the file and which application-specific initialization settings are required. The resulting states are instantiated on reproducible Ubuntu virtual machines for task synthesis and trajectory collection. 3.2.2 ENVIRONMENT-GROUNDED TASK SYNTHESIS Given the diverse desktop environments constructed above, we next translate environment diversity into training-task diversity. Each synthesis episode first samples target application and then selects compatible artifacts via the applicationartifact compatibility graph, thereby instantiating coherent and executable task context. Relying primarily on model priors tends to produce generic, repetitive instruction patterns and underutilize the state diversity of instantiated environments at scale. We therefore ground instruction generation in active exploration of the current environment. To avoid repeatedly covering familiar functionality, we maintain global application memory that records functions previously exercised for each application and exposes this history during subsequent exploration, encouraging broader coverage over time. The Exploration Agent receives this memory together with application metadata, exact file paths, launch configuration, tutorial, and initial screenshot, and performs short non-destructive exploration restricted to opening, clicking, scrolling, and terminating. Based on the observed artifact content and application state, it proposes realistic user instruction together with its initialization configuration and observable success conditions, without prescribing GUI/code solution or revealing answer-critical information. To make synthesized tasks consistently verifiable, we adopt an everything-is-a-file abstraction in which terminal conditions are mapped, whenever possible, to inspectable file representations, and evaluator synthesis selects rule-based, VLM-based, or hybrid checks according to their observability. Verification specifies the desired terminal state without constraining how it is reached, allowing the same task to be completed through GUI interaction, code execution, or their combination. We decouple the instruction proposal from evaluator synthesis. Once an instruction proposal is accepted, its instruction and success conditions are frozen and passed to an independent Evaluator Agent, which compiles the corresponding verification logic. Programmatically observable conditions are evaluated primarily with rule-based checks over VM files and command-line state, while visual conditions that cannot be reliably recovered programmatically are handled with VLM-based evaluation. Instructions are checked for reachability, unambiguity, realism, and sufficient verification conditions, while evaluators must compile and assign zero reward to the initial state. Invalid evaluators are repaired when possible. Each validated instruction and evaluator then constitutes task, after which semantically Instructions and evaluators are validated separately in the pipeline. 5 near-duplicate tasks are removed. Together, environment-grounded synthesis and file-backed verification produce scalable pool of verifiable tasks shared by SFT trajectory collection and online RL. Data infrastructure details are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3.3.1 SFT COLD START
sections.content: Most open-source CUAs used as base models have previously been trained primarily for GUI-only interaction. They may possess visual understanding, coordinate grounding, and low-level control, but have not learned the new decision boundary created when code execution becomes an equally valid action. Merely adding code tool expands the action space without supplying routing prior for when to remain in the GUI, when to switch to code, and when to return to the interface for verification; it can even disrupt already learned GUI behavior. SFT therefore serves as cold start in our pipeline: it establishes the action semantics of the unified tool schema and distills from teacher trajectories coarse but usable GUI/code routing policy. We collect SFT trajectories on tasks produced by the data infrastructure described in Section 3.2, using Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) as the teacher model with both Computer Use and Bash Tool enabled. The resulting trajectories are then postprocessed and normalized into the OS-Helix action schema. Each trajectory is scored by its evaluator, using the teacher model itself when visual judgment is required, and the resulting score serves as the primary signal for rejection sampling. We further apply filtering pipeline to remove malformed tool calls, schema-mismatched actions, and trajectories that fail evaluator or quality checks, yielding set of high-quality SFT samples. Training hyperparameters and data-mixture details are provided in Appendix C.1. 3.3.2 AGENTIC RL WITH STEP-BALANCED GSPO We first build cross-node environment management system that monitors and manages over one hundred Ubuntu sandbox environments across multiple standalone machines. The system exposes unified port to the training side and internally dispatches requests to the environments. We then perform online RL on carefully filtered generated tasks with rule-based evaluators only, further improving model performance. Each rollout interacts with live desktop environment, and the paired evaluator score serves as the sole outcome reward signal. If an assistant turn contains an unparsable tool call or any other invalid action-format error, that assistant response is isolated as an invalid sample and assigned reward of 0, even if the remaining trajectory could receive positive evaluator score. We use three efficiency mechanisms to make online RL feasible under costly desktop interaction. First, we adopt an asynchronous RL pipeline that allows the rollout policy to lag behind the latest policy by at most one version, enabling environment interaction and policy optimization to run in parallel. Second, we maintain per-task success-rate estimates and bias sampling toward tasks near the current capability frontier, down-weighting tasks that are already too easy or remain too difficult. Third, we apply bounded sliding-window visual-context segmentation to control context length and sample growth. Rollouts are split into segments and each segment can contain multiple assistant actions that contribute to loss. We apply the same sliding-window segmentation logic during rollout inference to maintain consistency between training and inference. In our preliminary RL experiments, standard GSPO exhibited systematic drift toward codeintensive behavior as shown in Figure 4. Specifically, as training progresses, the model increasingly favors code-related actions, ultimately resulting in slight performance degradation relative to the initial SFT checkpoint. Within mixed GUI/code training sample, code action typically contains substantially more assistant tokens than GUI click or keystroke. Standard GSPO averages tokenlevel log-importance weights over all valid assistant tokens in the sample. Thus, even when long code action constitutes only one of several GUI and code steps, it can dominate both the samplelevel importance ratio and the clipping decision. This motivates an aggregation in which the weight assigned to each action step in the sample-level log-ratio is no longer determined by its token count. Step-balanced GSPO modifies only the aggregation of the sample-level ratio. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP Evaluation Benchmarks. Our evaluation centers on desktop environments, employing OSWorld1 (Xie et al., 2024; 2025) as our primary benchmark, which comprises 369 real-world tasks across five domains in an Ubuntu environment. Following common practice (Xie et al., 2024), we exclude the 8 Google Drive tasks, yielding final set of 361 tasks. We report mean success rate as the primary metric. Beyond the Ubuntu environment, we additionally report results on WindowsAgentArena (Bonatti et al., 2024) to evaluate cross-platform transfer to Windows. 1In this paper, OSWorld refers to OSWorld-Verified. 7 Models and Baselines. We instantiate OS-Helix from Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35BA3B (Qwen Team, 2026a). For broader context, we also report representative agentic frameworks, general-purpose models, specialist models, and matched backbone baselines. Implementation Details. For task synthesis, we use Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) for the Exploration and Evaluator Agents, and GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026) for an independent quality review agent. For SFT, we train for one epoch on 31K successful filtered desktop samples synthesized by our pipeline and 40K general-purpose multimodal samples spanning code, reasoning, and related domains. For RL, we initialize from the dense OS-Helix-27B checkpoint and conduct 1,000-step training run using rule-based evaluators as reward signals. Complete data details are provided in Appendix B, while training details are provided in Appendix C. Unless otherwise specified, each evaluation episode is capped at 50 interaction steps and retains up to 8 historical screenshots (resolution 1504x832) together with the full textual interaction history. All reproduced baseline results are evaluated using the same harness and environment configuration.

sections.content: Accuracy versus efficiency. In Figure 3, evaluator scores above 0.5 are counted as successes and scores below 0.5 as failures. Panel (a) reports mean interaction steps. All tasks and Own successes use each runs complete and successful task sets, respectively, whereas Joint successes and Joint failures retain only shared tasks on which all three policies have the same binary outcome, controlling for task-composition differences. Panel (b) reports cumulative Success@K on OSWorld. Across the full set, successful episodes, and outcome-matched subsets, OS-Helix-27B uses fewer interactions while covering more successes under small step budgets. Learned modality routing therefore improves both execution efficiency and task coverage, an effect not reproduced by enabling code only at inference time. 9 Figure 3: Execution efficiency on OSWorld. Figure 4: Training dynamics, scaling, and coverage analysis. Why step balance matters. Panel (a) of Figure 4 uses the fraction of actions invoking code at each online RL update as behavioral diagnostic. Under the same training setup, standard GSPO progressively drifts toward code-intensive behavior, whereas Step-balanced GSPO remains lower and more stable over the shared observed horizon. Panel (b) reports repeated-sampling coverage. Compared with the SFT policy, OS-Helix-27B-RL improves Pass@1 from 62.75% to 66.44% (+3.69 points) and Pass@3 from 70.88% to 76.44% (+5.56 points), with the latter supported by pairedbootstrap confidence interval of 95% [2.24,8.97]. The larger gain under Pass@3 indicates that RL does more than strengthen single preferred trajectory and increases the probability of discovering distinct successful trajectories across independent attempts. Training scaling and data distributions. Panels (c)(f) of Figure 4 further examine the performance scaling and instruction distributions. Panel (c) reports success for the Work. category and the overall average across checkpoints from the first SFT epoch. Panel (d) holds the desktop data fixed and varies the fraction of the 40K general-purpose multimodal pool from 0% to 100%. Both sets of curves improve overall as the supervision grows, indicating complementary contributions from hybrid trajectories and general-purpose data. Panels (e)(f) show kernel-density estimates of these per-task statistics. We encode each instruction with text-embedding-3-large (OpenAI, 2024), L2-normalize the embedding, and compute cosine similarity by vector dot product. The cross-corpus similarity to OSWorld is comparable to OSWorlds internal-instruction similarity, indicating limited instruction-level overlap. Together with domain-removal ablation in Table 3, this provides complementary evidence against direct instruction overlap or reliance on data from the evaluated domains. Meanwhile, the synthesized corpus exhibits higher but still broadly spread internal-similarity distribution, suggesting that it captures shared, transferable desktop-task structure rather than collapsing to narrow instruction template family.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present OS-Helix, native hybrid computer-using agent trained end-to-end through scalable executable desktop task synthesis, hybrid SFT, and Step-balanced GSPO online RL, designed to natively coordinate heterogeneous GUI and code actions within single policy. On OSWorld-Verified, 10 OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their matched Qwen3.5 hybrid baselines, while OS-Helix-27B-RL further improves by 42.9% to reach 66.44% success. OS-Helix-27B-RL also transfers to WindowsAgentArena with 63.87% success, surpassing GPT-5-based framework methods on both benchmarks. Ablations and behavioral analyses show that SFT provides the main gain, hybrid supervision outperforms GUI-only supervision at fixed scale, and learned routing improves both execution efficiency and task coverage beyond code access alone. Under matched RL settings, Step-balanced GSPO outperforms standard GSPO and mitigates its drift toward code-intensive behavior, while RL increases Pass@3 from 70.88% to 76.44%, indicating broader discovery of successful trajectories across independent attempts. These findings establish native GUI/code coordination as learnable hybrid paradigm and provide reproducible foundation for further research on hybrid computer-using agents.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In the preparation of this manuscript, we utilized LLMs to generate synthetic datasets, to refine the writing (including grammar and spelling corrections), to draft sections of the paper, and to assist with the preliminary derivation of mathematical formulas in Appendix E. The authors reviewed and take responsibility for the research design, experiments, analysis, claims, and final presentation.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work does not involve human-subject studies or the collection of private data from real users. We study training methods for general-purpose computer-using agents, and conduct all trajectory collection, reinforcement learning, and evaluation in controlled, isolated Ubuntu virtual machines. The VMs use fixed application versions and curated local file library, and are separated from personal host files and credentials. This setup reduces the risk that exploratory actions during research inadvertently modify host state or access unauthorized resources. Although the experiments themselves present no substantial direct ethical risk, deploying agents with combined GUI interaction and code execution on real devices raises important safety and privacy concerns. Such agents can continuously observe screen content, modify local files, and execute Python or Bash, and may therefore encounter personally identifiable information, confidential documents, or authentication credentials. They may also be exposed to prompt injection through interface content or external files. Code actions further increase the potential impact of erroneous behavior or malicious workflows. The isolated experimental setting used in this work does not resolve these deployment-time risks. Real-world deployment should follow least-privilege and safety-by-design principles. These include granular permissions over applications, directories, networks, and code execution; explicit human confirmation before irreversible, credential-bearing, or otherwise high-impact operations; runtime policy checks, sandboxed execution, audit logs, and post-action verification; and data minimization and sanitization for screenshots, trajectories, and tool outputs. Users should retain the ability to define and revoke the agents authority, with sensitive applications such as banking, private communication, and credential management inaccessible by default. Because general-purpose automation is inherently dual use, future CUA research should advance capabilities together with systematic red teaming, interpretable action auditing, and reliable human takeover mechanisms.

sections.title: A LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: OS-Helix is an initial step toward native GUI/code hybrid computer use, with remaining limitations centered primarily on computational and API resource constraints. First, desktop environments are difficult to scale comprehensively: even an applicationartifact desktop infrastructure spanning diverse applications cannot cover the full diversity of real user machines, private artifacts, application versions, and personalized configurations. Future work should further expand the application and artifact ecosystem and study broader randomization of system states and user configurations while preserving reproducibility. Second, automatic verification remains imperfect. Unlike software engineering tasks, where gold final states can be obtained deterministically, automated CUA task synthesis under limited resources cannot reliably capture ground-truth terminal statestasks may therefore be subject to feasibility risks, and the resulting evaluators carry intrinsic brittleness. Concretely, rule-based evaluators reliably cover many file-backed tasks but require careful construction and often depend on specific application versions or export formats; more fundamentally, even when an agents execution is semantically near-correct, inconsistent strictness in file-attribute checks can reduce the score to zero. Rubric-based partial scoring, adopted in several recent works including ours, partially alleviates this issue but does not resolve it entirely. VLM-based evaluators extend coverage to textual outputs and visual outcomes, yet may miss fine-grained discrepancies; more critically, due to their inherent brittleness, existing RL engineering practice typically excludes VLM-based scoring from the reward signal altogether, concentrating construction effort on rule-based evaluatorswhich in turn constrains the types and diversity of tasks that can be incorporated into training. Future work should develop stronger evaluator-generation, repair, and validation pipelines, and systematically study cross-evaluator agreement as well as robustness to reward hacking. Third, our agentic RL experiments are subject to certain limitations imposed by available computational resources. RL training was conducted only on the dense 27B model with relatively conservative hyperparameter settings; the total number of training steps was likewise constrained, precluding systematic investigation of the scaling behavior of agentic RL. For OS-Helix-35B-A3B, despite its strong performance in SFT experiments, the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture introduces non-trivial additional challenges in training-inference consistency and optimization stability during agentic RL, making it difficult to support this training pipeline reliably under current resource conditions. We regard more thorough exploration of RL training dynamics and scaling laws, together with stable extension of Step-balanced GSPO to larger MoE computer-using agents, as an important direction for future work. Beyond scaling, we believe the community is now at an inflection point where recursive selfimprovement (RSI) deserves serious consideration. As CUA models attain meaningful level of general computer-use capability, the model itself can serve as its own teacher: rolling out interaction trajectories on existing tasks, providing the training signal for the next iteration, and progressively improving through this self-bootstrapping loop. Rather than relying solely on human demonstration or externally curated data, such paradigm allows the agent to continuously generate its own training trajectories with growing quality as capability improves and feed them back into subsequent training rounds. We view this self-evolving, teacher-free training paradigm as one of the most promising long-term directions for advancing CUA agents. Finally, many existing desktop benchmarks were originally designed for GUI-only agents, with task design, reference solutions, and evaluation functions all implicitly centered on visual interaction paths. Although their tasks can often be completed with hybrid strategies, existing evaluators may not capture every valid GUI/code solution. Furthermore, using success rate as the sole metric is overly coarse: it neither distinguishes whether the agent selected the more efficient modality nor captures potential safety risks inherent to hybrid execution, such as unintended side effects of code execution or inadvertent system-level operations. particularly promising complementary direction is the migration and adaptation of existing general-purpose agent benchmarks such as GDPval (Patwardhan et al., 2026) and Agents Last Exam (Sun et al., 2026b) into GUI environments. These benchmarks are inherently designed around authentic artifact manipulation and complex reasoning tasks, and thus naturally encompass diverse environment states and authentic artifacts. The comparison is organized along the axis of synthesis coverage rather than data scale or maturity. The broader contribution of OS-Helix is to extend exploration-grounded task generation toward artifact-grounded executable desktop-state construction: the pipeline jointly addresses K/E/C grounding, application scaling, authentic artifact-backed state initialization, and executable rule-based evaluation within single coherent framework. Concretely, an application artifact compatibility graph organizes valid pairings of application configurations and supported artifact types or file formats, enabling reproducible initial states to be instantiated systematically. The evaluator pipeline verifies persistent terminal outcomes rather than constraining the action sequence, supporting diverse task objectives and evaluation criteria across application domains and providing the infrastructure for subsequent hybrid-policy training. Cross-application task synthesis is currently realized as limited prototype, reflected by the partial symbol in the table; extending this component into larger and more systematically characterized collection remains an explicit direction for future work. Works such as Qwen-CUA and Qwen-UIAgent have demonstrated more extensive coverage of long-horizon and cross-application workflows at scale, and those dimensions represent clear avenues for subsequent expansion of OS-Helix. B.3 FINAL STATE MATERIALIZATION Our everything-is-a-file abstraction treats the file system as common inspection interface rather than as restriction on where task state must originate. terminal condition may initially reside in downloaded web page, an in-memory application state, an unsaved layout, or persistent user artifact. We attempt to materialize the relevant condition into VM-resident file representation whenever this can preserve the semantics needed for evaluation: web state may be downloaded or serialized locally, an in-memory result may be exported, and an answer may be written to structured or plain-text file. This externalization separates the location of state from its verifiable representation and allows heterogeneous desktop objectives to share common evaluation interface. The materialization step is not uniformly lossless. Some conditions, such as exact document structure, metadata, or serialized application state, admit faithful programmatic inspection; others depend on rendered layout, canvas appearance, transient UI state, or content for which serialization does not preserve the relevant evidence. Evaluator selection therefore reflects an observability trade-off: rule-based checks are used when deterministic file or command representation captures the required semantics, VLM-based checks are used when visual or otherwise non-serializable evidence is essential, and hybrid evaluators combine the two when they provide complementary evidence. B.4 INSTRUCTION AND EVALUATOR SYNTHESIS DETAILS The primary task-synthesis pipeline instantiates states through the applicationartifact compatibility graph. The pipeline then follows one-way information flow: application and artifact configurations determine the initialization context; the Exploration Agent produces structured instruction proposal and textual success conditions; the independent Evaluator Agent compiles the frozen conditions into rule-based or visual checks; and each independently validated instruction-evaluator pair enters the task pool. Application-centered initialization. For each application, we record canonical name, version, supported artifact types and file formats, launch commands, and initialization templates, and use these fields to build the applicationartifact compatibility graph. Each synthesis episode first restores controlled VM snapshot and samples primary application, then selects zero or more compatible artifacts through the graph according to the applications initialization templates. For every sampled pre-existing artifact, initialization creates VM-resident, evaluator-only golden copy before task execution while leaving the original path as the active task target; this copy is bound to the task configuration and may serve as the expected reference in subsequent content or structural comparisons. The system then provides the Exploration Agent with application metadata, exact file paths, launch configuration, an application tutorial, global application memory, and an initial screenshot. The following partial PyCharm configuration illustrates how application metadata connects application initialization with artifact-library sampling. The version field fixes the application version assumed by task synthesis, trajectory collection, and evaluator implementation, while type declares the artifact or project types that the application can directly consume. The two entries in commands are alternative initialization templates: the first launches an empty application, and the second launches the application with sampled artifact. The position-aligned values in random are normalized into initialization probabilities; hence [10, 90] assigns approximately 10% probability to an empty PyCharm launch and 90% to fileor project-backed launch. When the second template is selected, the system randomly samples an absolute file path whose type is compatible with type from the artifact library and substitutes it for PATH before executing the command. The related app and related type fields retain compatibility relations among applications and artifact types for selecting conventional companion applications and for the graph-guided cross-application prototype. 23 This declarative configuration is what makes application scaling reproducible rather than collection of ad hoc launch scripts. Adding an application requires specifying its version, launch procedures, supported artifact types, initialization probabilities, and optional relations to companion applications. The compatibility graph then filters valid applicationartifact pairings before an episode is instantiated in fixed VM, allowing new applications and artifact types to expand the executable state space while preserving initialization and sampling semantics. Example Application Configuration: PyCharm "pycharm": { "version": "PyCharm 2025.3.3", "type": [ "py", "project_folder" ], "commands": [ [ [["pycharm-community"]] ], [ [["pycharm-community", "PATH"]] ] ], "random": [10, 90], "related_app": [ "vscode", "gitkraken" ], "related_type": [ "py", "project_folder" ] } Grounded instruction proposal. To avoid repeatedly covering familiar functionality, we maintain global application memory that records functions previously exercised for each application and expose it during subsequent exploration. When additional interface information is needed, the Exploration Agent may perform short non-destructive inspection using only open, click, scroll, and done. Keyboard and free-form text input are unavailable to avoid mutating the known initial state. It then proposes goal-oriented instruction and fine-grained success conditions for evaluator synthesis. The resulting instruction record contains fields such as snapshot, versioned related apps, instruction, config, complexity, category, success criteria, and evaluation requirements text. The instruction field is the core user-facing task specification. The snapshot, related apps, and config fields are determined during initialization and record the reproducible environment context. The category field is generated by the Exploration Agent together with the instruction and is divided into three groups. app only denotes tasks centered on application or system functionality, such as changing software or user settings. file only denotes tasks centered on processing input files whose final deliverables are file artifacts. mixed denotes tasks that involve both. The complexity field estimates the length of pure-GUI solution. We label tasks with 515 steps as easy, tasks with 1540 steps as medium, and tasks with more than 40 steps as complex. The success criteria field lists the terminal conditions that must hold after successful task completion. The evaluation requirements text field translates those conditions into concrete checks for evaluator synthesis, such as which file, slide, field, format, or application state should be inspected. The instruction states non-answer constraints such as locations, scope, ordering, quantity, format, and filenames. Exact observed values are retained only in these hidden success and evaluation fields. Evaluator synthesis. Evaluator synthesis begins only after an instruction proposal has been accepted and is performed by an independent Evaluator Agent in separate context. Its inputs are the frozen instruction fields, initialization configuration, success criteria, and textual evaluation requirements. The Evaluator Agent may generate only the verification specification and cannot revise the instruction or proposal metadata. rule-based evaluator comprises one or more self-contained Python judge functions. Each function declares its required imports locally, can run independently, accepts result and expected as inputs, and typically evaluates one well-defined subgoal. Either 24 input may be supplied by vm file as VM-resident file or by vm command line as commandobservable state. When initialization creates local golden copy, expected may refer to it for content or structural comparison. When the target can be encoded directly in the rule, expected may be empty. Each judge accumulates rubric-based score over fine-grained completion items It returns value in [0, 1], with zero for no satisfied items and one for with assigned weights. complete satisfaction; if execution raises an exception, it returns the score accumulated before the exception. The evaluator relies only on VM-resident artifacts and deterministic rules, without external or cloud-hosted golden assets, and checks the final artifacts content, structure, formatting, metadata, or configuration state. fully rules express deterministic When sets the need rule judge=true without enabling visual judgment. When visual layout, canvas state, unparsable application-internal state, or dynamic web content is indispensable for verification, it may set need vlm judge=true. In this case, the VLM judge receives the agents execution trajectory as input, and vlm desc specifies the visual objects, attributes, and spatial relations to inspect in that trajectory. conditions, evaluator success the Rule-based and VLM-based judgments may both be used for task verification, but their scores are recorded separately. For task with multiple rule judges, the rule-based score is the mean of the individual rule-judge scores, whereas the VLM-based score is produced independently by visual judgment. During SFT filtering, the two scores are thresholded separately, and task is retained only when both its rule-based score and VLM-based score meet their respective thresholds (both 0.8). As described in Section 4.1, RL uses only tasks with rule-based evaluators to provide reward signals. This design avoids the brittleness and computational cost of VLM judgment and prevents the calibration mismatch that could arise from averaging the two score types directly. Although both scores lie in [0, 1], rule-based scores are derived from fine-grained, explicitly weighted completion items, whereas VLM scores generally reflect coarser and more subjective judgment scale. The two scores therefore do not have interchangeable numerical semantics. Consequently, VLM judgment is used primarily to cover programmatic observability gaps during SFT-stage filtering. Instruction and evaluator filtering. Filtering first checks whether the JSON schema, getter arguments, and Python code can be parsed and compiled statically. The system then initializes the environment from the initialization configuration and executes the evaluator before any action. The initial-state score must be zero, as nonzero score indicates reward leakage. An independent review model next scores instruction quality and evaluator quality separately. The former assesses whether the instruction is unambiguous, reachable, and realistic, while the latter assesses whether the evaluator covers all success conditions, is sufficiently strict, and resists reward hacking. An instruction below the quality threshold is removed directly. If the instruction is valid but its evaluator fails an automated check or quality review, the system uses the previous evaluator and its failure information as revision context, regenerates the evaluator, and repeats the full validation and scoring procedure. The associated proposal is removed only after multiple repair attempts remain unsuccessful. After correctness filtering, we use embedding similarity to remove near-duplicate instructions generated across batches, producing the task pool used for training stages. The RL task pool is then built by rolling out trajectories with the SFT-trained model on this pool and keeping tasks of moderate difficulty. Prototype cross-application extension. Beyond the applicationsystem compositions in the primary task pool, we implemented and began collecting more structured form of cross-application task synthesis. The prototype uses the related app field in the application configurations to construct an application graph. Applications serve as nodes, while edges encode compositional relations induced by shared artifact types or file formats, convertible intermediate artifacts, or complementary workflows. This graph provides structured prior for composing applications rather than treating all application combinations as equally plausible. For each task, the system first specifies target number of applications, such as three, randomly samples primary application, and then samples subsequent applications from its neighboring nodes. After each selection, the neighbors of the selected nodes are added to the candidate frontier, allowing the application set to expand along graph structure. To prevent the graph from overly constraining the composition space, each sampling step retains small-probability jump mechanism that ignores graph connectivity and samples an application uniformly from the broader inventory. Artifact selection follows corresponding compositional 25 procedure and may introduce zero or more related artifacts. This setting expands the exploration space and requires the Exploration Agent to additionally infer cross-application dependencies, including the execution order and the transfer of artifacts or intermediate results, before proposing long-horizon instruction. We have already generated small number of such prototype tasks and included them in the task pool. Their current scale is insufficient for systematic evaluation of cross-application capabilities, so future work will expand the collection and study its effect on long-horizon execution across applications. Percentages are computed from the raw counts for each panel and displayed to two decimal places. C.2 GSPO RL CONFIGURATION Our RL system is built on the asynchronous Slime framework (Zhu et al., 2025), augmented with custom training logic for online desktop interaction. Each rollout collection contains 8 prompts and samples 8 trajectories per prompt, yielding 64 rollout samples per collection. We use maximum of 50 GUI interaction steps, rollout temperature of 0.5, and maximum response length of 10,240. Tasks are dynamically sampled according to an exponential moving average of their success rates. SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) serves as the rollout backend, while Megatron (Shoeybi et al., 2019) is used for policy training. The RL objective is Step-balanced GSPO, with disabled KL divergence and equal weights of 1.0 for GUI and code steps. The full configuration is listed in Table 11. C.3 ONLINE RL SAMPLING, SEGMENTATION, AND REWARDS Uniform task sampling is inefficient for online CUA training because many rollouts are spent on tasks that are either already solved or still out of reach. Following the frontier-sampling intuition in prior ScaleCUA (Lv et al., 2026), we maintain success-rate estimate for each task and bias sampling toward tasks near the current capability frontier. 27 For each task i, we initialize ˆpi = 0.5. After each update window, if ni new rollouts are available for task i, we update its success-rate estimate by ˆpi αˆpi + (1 α) 1 ni ni(cid:88) j=1 1[ri,j > 0], where α is the EMA retention coefficient, consistent with the task-sampling EMA parameter in Table 11. The task sampling weight is then computed with Gaussian kernel, (cid:18) wi = exp (ˆpi µ)2 2σ2 (cid:19) , We set the target success rate to µ = 0.5 and the bandwidth to σ = 0.25. Thus tasks with very high or very low estimated success rates receive lower weights, while tasks near the target success rate are sampled more often. To control visual-context length, we use bounded sliding-window strategy. Each rollout maintains history of 510 screenshots. When the history exceeds 10 screenshots, we save the current stream as training segment, discard the five oldest screenshots, retain the five most recent screenshots, and resume collecting observations. Only assistant responses generated while the retained screenshot history lies in this 510 range contribute to the loss. Earlier context tokens are retained only as conditioning information with loss mask 0. Rewards come only from the paired environment evaluator, env.evaluate. We do not use auxiliary format rewards or handcrafted step-level rewards. For valid trajectories and segments, evaluator scores are real values in [0, 1]. If an assistant response contains an unparsable tool call, an action outside the allowed schema, or another invalid action-format failure, that response is extracted as separate invalid sample and assigned reward 0, even if the remaining trajectory could otherwise obtain positive task-level score. This prevents malformed actions from receiving accidental positive credit through later recovery.

sections.title: D EXTRA EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: D.1 TRANSFER TO WINDOWSAGENTARENA Table 12 reports additional results for the 27B backbone and its corresponding OS-Helix variants on WindowsAgentArena, providing evidence of transfer from the Ubuntu-based training setting to this Windows benchmark. We retain the GUI and Hybrid baselines from the main experiments to preserve the same comparison between action-space access and learned hybrid behavior. Of particular note, since the operating system environment is Windows, we restrict Code actions to Python only, excluding the use of Bash. When Cmd/PowerShell commands would otherwise be required, system calls are instead issued directly within Python; this adaptation is implemented via prompt revision. Despite the absence of Windows-specific training data, OS-Helix improves on this benchmark. The SFT-only OS-Helix-27B raises the matched GUI backbone from 40.82% to 57.95%, gain of 17.13 absolute points, and the RL variant reaches 63.87%, exceeding the GUI baseline by 23.05 points and the Hybrid baseline by 7.46 points. The unadapted Hybrid baseline also improves substantially over GUI (56.41% versus 40.82%), while OS-Helix-27B adds further 1.54 points. These comparisons provide benchmark-specific evidence that learned GUI/code routing transfers to WindowsAgentArena under the reported Python-only prompt adaptation. The remaining gap is also diagnostic. In contextual comparisons reported on the same benchmark, OS-Helix-27B-RL slightly exceeds OS-Symphony w/ GPT-5 and Agent S3 w/ GPT-5 under the shared 50-step budget. As result, the model can under-learn when to stop and declare infeasibility, often continuing until the maximum interaction budget is exhausted. D.2 ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS The diagnostic experiments in this subsection are conducted with Qwen3-series models (Bai et al., 2025), which differ from the Qwen3.5-series base models used in the experiments above. The training data and data recipe, however, are kept exactly the same, so the comparison isolates how the same OS-Helix training signal behaves on different backbone family. All experiments in this subsection use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) only and do not include reinforcement learning (RL). Accordingly, the analyses below study the transferability of the learned GUI/code behavior and the information content of the SFT data, rather than the contribution of online policy optimization. D.2.1 GROUNDING ABILITY CHECK Table 13 reports grounding benchmark performance on Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and an OS-Helix32B variant with the same data recipe as our Qwen3.5-series models. The reproduced base model obtains 61.35 on OSWorld-G (Xie et al., 2026) and 95.05 on ScreenSpot-V2 (Wu et al., 2025), while OS-Helix-32B obtains 57.21 and 93.47, respectively. This decrease is expected rather than contradictory to our main results. The training objective does not only optimize pixel grounding; it also teaches the model to format tool calls, reason over files, invoke code when programmatic execution is more reliable, and recover from multi-step environment feedback. In this sense, the model reallocates some capacity away from isolated grounding benchmarks toward hybrid desktop execution. The key observation is that even when pure grounding slightly decreases, code-capable action selection can compensate for this loss in end-to-end tasks 30 by avoiding brittle pixel-level interactions and solving precise file or data operations through the operating system. D.2.2 BACKBONE REPLACEMENT ANALYSIS To test whether the training signal transfers beyond the original backbone, we repeat the SFT experiment with Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking. Table 14 reports the complete OSWorld breakdown; arrows in the OS-Helix rows denote absolute-point changes relative to the Qwen3-VL baseline under the same Setting. With the Instruct backbone, adding Code without training hybrid policy slightly decreases the baseline from 34.17% (GUI) to 32.68% (Hybrid). After SFT, however, OS-Helix-32B reaches 50.56%, +17.88-point improvement over the matched Hybrid baseline. With the Thinking backbone, the unadapted Hybrid baseline is somewhat better than GUI (42.88% versus 39.08%), but OS-Helix-32B-Thinking still improves it by +8.79 points to 51.67%. Thus, the result isolates two effects: Code availability is not itself sufficient for reliable hybrid execution, while the SFT training signal transfers across both backbones and converts the available action space into substantially stronger policy. The domain-level changes clarify what is learned. For Instruct, OS-Helix-32B improves all five domains over the matched Hybrid baseline. The corresponding gains in OS, Office, Daily, Prof., and Work. are 16.67, 19.66, 16.83, 12.24, and 19.76 points, respectively. The gains are therefore broad rather than being explained by single application family, with the largest improvements in Office and multi-application tasks in the Work. category. This pattern is consistent with learning cross-step state management and modality routing, rather than simply improving visual grounding on isolated screens. For Thinking, the gains remain broad in OS (+8.33), Office (+11.94), Daily (+11.40), and Work. (+9.40), but Prof. decreases by 2.83 points. The single negative domain is useful qualification: backbone replacement does not erase model-specific priors, and SFT can redistribute capability unevenly across application families. Nevertheless, the positive average and the gains across the OS, Office, Daily, and Work. categories show that the central hybrid behavior is not tied to one backbones pretrained tool-use bias. These results also strengthen the distinction between action-space access and policy learning in the main claim. The Instruct baseline provides controlled counterexample in which the same model becomes slightly worse when Code is merely exposed at inference time. In contrast, the trained model gains most strongly on domains where successful execution requires coordinating GUI observations, executable operations, and persistent task state. The improvement should therefore be interpreted as evidence for learned coordination and routing, not as an artifact of giving the model an additional tool. D.2.3 TRAINING RECIPE AND CONTEXT ANALYSIS We next isolate how the structure of demonstrations and test-time history affects performance, using Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct with OSWorld. The normal recipe reaches 50.56%. Removing CoT from training and retaining actions only reduces performance to 37.74% (-12.82 points), while keeping the training data unchanged but removing CoT from the inference context yields 37.82% (-12.74 points). The near-identical degradation is important: the reasoning trace is not merely an auxiliary training target. It also functions as an execution-time state representation that helps the model maintain intent, resolve intermediate observations, and select between GUI and code actions across multistep execution. Removing only historical CoT is less damaging, but still lowers the average to 43.22% (-7.34 points). This partial recovery indicates that the current-step decision can retain useful local information, yet removing the accumulated reasoning history weakens temporal credit assignment and state tracking. The effect is especially visible in the Work. category, where success falls from 38.54% to 28.87% without training CoT, 31.43% without inference CoT, and 31.30% without historical CoT. Multiapplication tasks therefore expose the central role of structured context most clearly: their difficulty lies not only in individual grounding decisions, but in preserving coherent plan while the active application and tool modality change. Finally, mixing in trajectories rejected during filtering reduces the score to 47.06% (-3.50 points). STEP-BALANCED GSPO DETAILS During reinforcement learning, training sample may contain multiple assistant responses that contribute to the policy loss, with each response corresponding to one action step. The optimization unit of training sample therefore need not coincide with an individual environment action step. In particular, the assistant span associated with code action step is often substantially longer than that associated with GUI step. The standard GSPO objective computes one sample-level importance ratio by aggregating token-level log-importance weights over all valid assistant tokens in the training sample (Zheng et al., 2025). Although this prevents sample from receiving larger sample-level weight solely because it contains more tokens, it does not equalize the contributions of different action steps within the same sample. As result, long code action can dominate both the sample-level ratio and the clipping decision even when it is only one of several actions in the training sample. This section formalizes the effect and derives step-balanced aggregation for the GSPO ratio. Our goal is to preserve GSPOs token-level importance weights and clipping structure while changing their sample-level aggregation to remove the deterministic dependence of an action steps aggregate gradient coefficient on its token count. Recent work has also studied the granularity of importance ratios for LLM policy optimization, including sequence-level GSPO (Zheng et al., 2025), subsentence-level ratios (Yang et al., 2025a), cumulative token ratios (Zhang et al., 2026b), and hybrid token/sequence ratios (Min et al., 2026). These methods differ from our setting at the objective level. SSPO assigns separate ratios to text fragments, but its published objective aggre32 gates fragments with token-length normalization and does not use environment-action boundaries or action-type weights. Rather, the longer serialized action contributes more token-level gradient terms under the same sample-level advantage and can therefore exert disproportionate influence on the update direction. The first is grounded in spreadsheet, whereas the second constructs and transfers persistent application configuration between recording tool and video editor. Together, they illustrate applicationartifact composition, environment-grounded task specification, and componentwise terminal verification in executable task records. Both use reviewed rule-based evaluators that assign partial terminal credit across independently verifiable task components. We reproduce the task metadata, complete instructions, and selected rule code to make these success conditions concrete. F.1 SYNTHESIS TASK CASE STUDY 1: OFFICE AND CODE WORKFLOW The first task spans LibreOffice Calc and VSCode. It starts from spreadsheet containing vehicle records, requires row-level categorization in the spreadsheet, and then asks for runnable Python audit script over the saved artifact. The task is labeled complex and estimated to require 30 interaction steps. F.3 AGENT BEHAVIOR CASE STUDY: GUICODE COORDINATION Figure 6 shows two successful trajectories in which OS-Helix coordinates GUI perception with code execution. These cases are intended to make the learned hybrid behavior concrete: the GUI is used where the task depends on the current application state or user-facing interface, while code is used where the same goal contains structured extraction, precise inspection, or repetitive operations. In the first case, the agent starts from the browser/PDF interface and uses the opened course material to infer the lecture-file URL pattern. Once this pattern is grounded by GUI observation, the agent switches to code and downloads the remaining weekly PDFs in loop. The important behavior is not simply that code is faster for downloading files, but that the code action is conditioned on information first obtained from the live GUI state. This illustrates complementary route in which GUI interaction resolves task-specific context and code then executes the scalable part of the workflow. In the second case, the agent inspects payment spreadsheet with code to identify students whose tuition has not been paid, then returns to the GUI to fill the e-mail recipients in the mail client. Here, code provides reliable structured filtering over tabular records, while GUI interaction completes the user-facing communication step. Together, the two examples show that the unified action space allows the policy to decompose task across modalities instead of committing to single interface throughout the trajectory. F.4 AGENT BEHAVIOR CASE STUDY: CROSS-MODALITY VERIFICATION Figure 7 presents two successful trajectories where one modality solves the task and the other verifies or repairs the result. This behavior is qualitatively different from merely choosing between GUI and code at the beginning of task: the agent can use the second modality as an intermediate feedback channel, detect mismatch between the intended and realized artifact, and then continue the trajectory with corrective action. In the spreadsheet-chart case, the agent first creates the requested clustered column chart with code. The subsequent GUI observation reveals that the produced chart only contains the Sales series and misses COGS, which would be difficult to notice from the code path alone without explicitly checking the rendered artifact. The agent then repairs the chart through code, producing the required 38 Figure 6: Successful GUIcode coordination cases. The top case first uses GUI observation to infer the URL pattern from an opened lecture slide, then uses code to download the remaining weekly PDFs. The bottom case uses code to extract payment records from spreadsheet and then returns to the GUI to fill the e-mail recipients. two-series visualization. This trace shows how GUI feedback can expose visual or application-level errors in code-generated artifacts and turn them into actionable corrections. In the slide-editing case, the agent performs the visible edits through GUI actions: it adds the note on the second slide and bolds the title. It then switches to code-based inspection of the saved presentation file to verify that the persistent artifact matches the instruction, including both the note text and the title formatting. This reverse direction, GUI for editing and code for validation, highlights that the benefit of the hybrid policy is bidirectional. Across the four successful traces in Appendix F.3 and Appendix F.4, the learned policy uses GUI and code as mutually checking and mutually enabling tools, supporting the claim that unified GUI/code action space yields complementary problem solving rather than replacing one modality with the other. F.5 FAILURE ANALYSIS: EVALUATION COVERAGE AND CROSS-MODALITY HANDOFFS Figure 8 presents two representative failures that expose gap between task specification and evaluation coverage, as well as state-handoff problem at the GUIcode boundary. Rather than indicating deficiency of either modality in isolation, these traces identify systematic challenges for hybrid policy in interpreting visual intent and maintaining persistent state across modalities. The top trace illustrates specificationevaluation coverage gap. Preserve the original formatting defines visual equivalence condition involving row banding, numeric display, borders, and other rendered attributes. When the instruction and validation signal do not fully characterize these attributes, or do not cover admissible solution paths equivalently, they create an underspecified proxy objective that can favor one modality. After code-based conversion, the agent detects mismatch through the GUI but attributes it to missing currency symbols, adding dollar signs rather than restoring the missing alternating row shading. natural GUI solution would select the Calc table and paste it into Writer, preserving its rendered appearance; serialization through code instead requires the visual formatting to be reconstructed explicitly. This case motivates aligning user intent, rendering semantics, and verification coverage so that the benchmark recognizes the full set of valid solutions without presupposing an action modality. The bottom trace exposes cross-modality state-handoff failure. The agent first completes the first subgoal correctly through the GUI. When code subsequently edits and saves the second subgoal, it writes only local disk-side state and does not incorporate the preceding modification that remains in the GUI-resident state. The GUI then mistakes the code-side save for global commit and selects Dont Save, discarding the correct update for the first subgoal. This is not planning failure on either subgoal in isolation; it is loss of persistence and commit semantics at the modality 39 Figure 7: Successful cross-modality solve-and-verify cases. The top case creates spreadsheet chart with code and then detects from the GUI that one data series is missing before repairing it. The bottom case completes slide editing through GUI actions and then verifies the saved file with code. transition. Reliable hybrid execution requires reconciling GUI-resident and code-side artifact states before handoff, while maintaining consistent representation of save scope and commit status. Figure 8: Representative failure cases. Top: In Calc-to-Writer transfer task requiring preservation of the original formatting, code-based conversion fails to retain the alternating row shading. The subsequent GUI observation identifies mismatch but misattributes it to missing currency symbols, so the agent adds dollar signs instead of restoring the table style. Bottom: After correctly completing the first PowerPoint subgoal through GUI actions, the agent edits and saves the second with code. The code-side save does not include the unsaved GUI state, and selecting Dont Save subsequently discards the earlier update. F.6 TRAJECTORY AUDIT We manually annotated 30 representative trajectories from the multi-step Work. category to examine whether modality transitions reflect task-grounded coordination. For each trajectory, we recorded the final outcome, compressed flow of the key GUI and code stages involved in coordination, and the purpose of any state or information handoff. The reported flow retains the principal stages that produce, consume, verify, or repair the reported handoff, while omitting repeated within-modality actions and transitions unrelated to that handoff. As summarized in Table 17, 27/30 trajectories contain grounded GUI/code handoff, including 22/30 in which one modality verifies or repairs 40 state produced by the other. The audited set contains 21 successful, 4 partially successful, and 5 failed trajectories. In four of the five failed trajectories, cross-modal state is transferred correctly and failure arises later from task incompletion or application/tool errors. The remaining trajectory exposes failed handoff: the PDF source observed in the GUI is replaced by different, unverified URL when code writes the spreadsheet. As the audit covers only representative task subset, the observed behavioral frequencies may not reflect the overall trends across the full benchmark. Moreover, the audited trajectories do not establish that the observed routing decisions are optimal. Even with these limitations, the examples directly show that OS-Helix performs task-grounded information handoffs and cross-modal verification and repair, using GUI and code as mutually enabling and checking mechanisms. This process-level evidence complements aggregate task scores, which capture outcomes rather than coordination behavior, and further supports our central claim that the model learns substantive cross-modal coordination.
